newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, grain prices rise on supply worries.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, grain prices rise on supply worries.

text.p: Coffee prices rose to their highest level in nearly a year on Monday and grains rose as worries about adequate supplies sparked speculator buying.
In other markets, lumber prices rose but copper, pork and gasoline prices fell. The Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures ended 0.33 point lower at 250.33.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, September coffee rose 4.20 cents per pound and closed at 136.45 cents, its highest close since September 6, 1995.
News on Monday of torrential rains and gale force winds in number two coffee producer Colombia rattled traders, but there was little early word of any damage to the coffee crop.
Of more immediate impact to traders was a shortage of quality coffee available for delivery against the September contract.
Speculative buying on Monday helped pressure holders of selling positions in the September contract to exit the market by buying contracts to cancel out their "short" positions.
"It is a squeeze, and shorts are being forced to cover," said Refco Inc. coffee analyst Ann Prendergast.
Exchange warehouse stocks of coffee have been declining for nearly two years and newly harvested supply from Brazil or Colombia won't arrive any time soon, analysts said.
Warehouse stocks fell to 34,736 bags in the week ended August 16, down from 1.25 million bags on December 30, 1994.
Meanwhile, the number of open contracts in the September delivery stood at 2,089 lots as of Friday -- the equivalent of over 500,000 bags of coffee.

Supply worries also boosted corn and soybean prices at the Chicago Board of Trade, with estimates of lower production this year by a trade group, The Professional Farmers of America, sparking buying by speculators.
December corn futures closed up 8-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.47-3/4 and November soybeans up 10-3/4 cents at $7.89-1/2.
"It's all Pro Farmer; their numbers boosted it and nothing else mattered today," said analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.

The trade group, which completed a crop tour of the Midwest Corn Belt states Friday, estimated the corn crop at 8.2 billion bushels, below the U.S. Agriculture Department's August 12 forecast for 8.695 billion bushels.
It pegged soybean production at 2.08 to 2.1 billion bushels, also well below the government's estimate of 2.3 billion.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange September lumber rose the $10 daily trading limit to close at $410.90 per thousand board feet, the highest price for lumber futures in 2-1/2 years.
Strong cash market demand and worries that Hurricane Edouard would stall transport or production fed buying, traders said.
Weather forecasters said Hurricane Edouard could hit Florida or the U.S. East Coast in five or six days.
"It gave shorts one more reason to cover," said Neil Schmaedick, forest products analyst for Smith Barney.
CME pork belly prices seesawed wildly after a quarterly government report on Friday put refrigerated stocks of frozen bellies, the raw material for bacon, at 20-year lows as of July.
August pork bellies shot up the 2.00 cent per pound daily limit early, then plummeted to close down the 2.00 cent limit at 90.525 cents.
Analysts cited increasing hog slaughter and weakness on cash markets as prompting the sharp reversal.
"The fresh market did not respond to the Cold Storage figure the way the futures did, so the fresh and futures market parted company," said Alaron Trading Corp analyst Chuck Levitt.
At the Commodity Exchange in New York, copper prices shrugged off possible labour problems at big mines to close lower. September copper ended at 91.10 cents a pound, down 0.60 cent.
Labour talks continue at Phelps Dodge Corp's Chino mine, where a labour contract expired June 30, and at Chile Copper Corp's Salvador mine, where the current deal ends September 1.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil and product prices closed sharply lower, with gasoline prices hardest hit, with traders citing profit-taking after the recent run-up.
"We are in the midst of a correction to relieve some of the overbought condition we are in technically," said Tom Bentz, a trader with ING Derivatives.

September unleaded gasoline closed down 1.60 cents to 61.62 cents a gallon Monday. Selling was spurred by news that Tosco Corp came a step closer to re-opening its 172,000 barrel-per-day Marcus Hook, Pennsylvania, refinery after it reached a labour pact with the union which represents the refinery workers.
October crude oil closed down 34 cents to $21.62 a barrel and September heating oil down 0.96 cent to 61.03 cents a gallon.
